description: Trigger discrimination for designing the flag SYSTEM once per product (this skill: store choice, interface, evaluation placement, targeting model, fail-safe mechanism, kill-switch propagation, change audit, debt hooks) vs one change's rollout on that system (feature-flag-rollout-strategist), permanent plan entitlements (plan-entitlement-architect), role permissions (authorization-matrix-designer), experiment design (ab-test-designer), deploy strategy and pipeline gates (ci-pipeline-architect, manual-only), control-plane structure (saas-platform-architect), cross-tenant leakage review (tenant-isolation-reviewer), general cache design (caching-strategy-designer), revoked access still honored (authority-invalidation-architect), and general page performance (frontend-perf-engineer). The hardest seam: the strategist picks each flag's safe VALUE; this skill designs the MECHANISM that falls back to it.

cases.prompt: Decide whether we build our own flag table or buy a flag service, where flags get evaluated, and what happens when the flag service is unreachable.
cases.note: SEAM CASE (primary, forward) — store choice, evaluation placement and outage behavior are properties of the flag system, decided once per product.
cases.reason: feature-flag-architect owns the system design; the strategist plans rollouts that run on whatever system exists.

cases.prompt: Plan the ramp for the new billing page from 1% to GA with auto-rollback and a date to delete the flag.
cases.note: SEAM CASE (primary, reverse) — stages, auto-rollback and removal date for one change are a rollout plan.
cases.reason: feature-flag-rollout-strategist owns how one change is de-risked; nothing here asks about the flag system.

cases.prompt: Our flag SDK blocks page render for three seconds whenever the flag service is down. Fix the design.
cases.note: HARD EDGE (mechanism) — the missing timeout, last-known-good cache and bootstrap are the fallback MECHANISM, which this skill designs for every flag.
cases.reason: The strategist picks each flag's safe value; this skill designs the mechanism that falls back to it. A render-blocking SDK is a mechanism defect, not a general page-performance problem: the slowdown exists only because the flag call waits on the network.

cases.prompt: Largest contentful paint is 4 s because of a 900 KB JavaScript bundle; fix it
cases.note: SEAM CASE (reverse) — a page-performance problem caused by bundle size, with no flag involved.
cases.reason: frontend-perf-engineer owns render performance, bundle size and Core Web Vitals; this skill only fixes render blocking caused by flag evaluation.

cases.prompt: If the flag service is unreachable, should the new checkout flag fall back to the old checkout or the new one?
cases.note: HARD EDGE (value, reverse) — choosing the safe value for one flag is part of that change's rollout plan.
cases.reason: The strategist picks each flag's safe value (usually the old behavior for a release flag); this skill only guarantees the system reaches it.

cases.prompt: Design our flag system's per-tenant override model so specific enterprise tenants can get early access until GA
cases.note: SEAM CASE (forward) — the per-tenant override data model (its precedence, server-side source of truth and tenant-qualified caching) is part of the flag system's targeting model, not a plan entitlement and not one ramp.
cases.reason: Early access that ends at GA is temporary exposure, which the flag targeting model carries; nothing is permanently included in a plan. Choosing WHICH tenants get early access and in what order for one ramp is feature-flag-rollout-strategist's job; the override data model every such ramp uses is this skill's.

cases.prompt: SSO should be permanently included in the Pro plan; right now a flag turns it on per account.
cases.note: SEAM CASE (reverse, hard) — a permanent plan inclusion currently faked with a flag belongs in the entitlement model.
cases.reason: plan-entitlement-architect owns what a plan includes; a flag standing in for an entitlement drifts from billing and must be moved out, not redesigned as a flag.

cases.prompt: Design the flag system so only on-call engineers can toggle production kill switches and every toggle is recorded.
cases.note: SEAM CASE (forward) — kill-switch authority per environment and the flag-change audit event are part of the flag system; the role definitions themselves are composed from authorization-matrix-designer.
cases.reason: The request is to design the flag system's control and audit path; this skill consumes the role definitions rather than authoring the whole permission matrix.

cases.prompt: Define which roles can view, edit and export tenant data, deny-by-default.
cases.note: SEAM CASE (reverse) — a roles × permissions matrix with no flag in sight.
cases.reason: authorization-matrix-designer owns role and permission design.

cases.prompt: Our experiments and our feature flags use two SDKs that bucket users differently; unify evaluation so assignment is consistent.
cases.note: SEAM CASE (forward) — one shared bucketing function across flags and experiments is evaluation mechanics of the flag system.
cases.reason: This skill guarantees consistent assignment; ab-test-designer owns an experiment's hypothesis, sizing and readout, none of which is asked.

cases.prompt: How many users do we need for the onboarding test to detect a 2% lift, and how long should it run?
cases.note: SEAM CASE (reverse) — sample size and duration are experiment design.
cases.reason: ab-test-designer owns power and duration; the flag system is irrelevant to the question.

cases.prompt: For our static marketing site plus app, should flags be baked in at build time or fetched at runtime?
cases.note: SEAM CASE (forward) — evaluation placement (build time vs runtime) is a flag-system decision, even though build time touches the pipeline.
cases.reason: Where flags evaluate is this skill's step; the pipeline stage graph is not being designed.

cases.prompt: Explicitly invoke ci-pipeline-architect. Add a canary deploy stage with automatic abort and a named-human promotion gate to our pipeline.
cases.note: SEAM CASE (reverse) — deploy strategy and promotion gates are pipeline design; ci-pipeline-architect is manual-only, so the user invokes it by name.
cases.reason: ci-pipeline-architect owns deploy strategies and pipeline gates; a canary DEPLOY is not a flag.

cases.prompt: What belongs in the control plane versus the data plane for our multi-tenant app?
cases.note: SEAM CASE (reverse) — platform structure, where feature flags are at most one listed capability.
cases.reason: saas-platform-architect owns the control-plane/data-plane split and the capability inventory; this skill designs the flag system once it is placed.

cases.prompt: Review our existing flag overrides and SDK payloads for cross-tenant leakage.
cases.note: SEAM CASE (reverse) — a leakage REVIEW of a real system, with flags as one surface.
cases.reason: tenant-isolation-reviewer reviews real systems for cross-tenant leakage across every surface; this skill designs, it does not audit.

cases.prompt: Some customers see beta features that were only switched on for a different customer until a few minutes pass. Our per-tenant flag overrides are cached in memory under the flag name. Redesign how our flag system targets and caches those overrides.
cases.note: SEAM CASE (proposal case 15; forward) — the cache in question holds evaluated flag values, and the fix is the targeting model's tenant-qualified key and precedence, which this skill owns.
cases.reason: Flag-value caching and keying are part of the flag system's targeting design; caching-strategy-designer owns general cache layers, not the flag evaluation model.

cases.prompt: Add a cache in front of our product-catalog endpoint: choose the layer, the TTLs, the key scheme and how invalidation works.
cases.note: SEAM CASE (reverse) — a general cache for an application endpoint with no flag involved.
cases.reason: caching-strategy-designer owns cache layer, TTL, key and invalidation design; this skill only caches evaluated flag values.

cases.prompt: We flipped the kill switch off but some instances kept serving the feature for ten minutes; design how flag changes reach every instance.
cases.note: SEAM CASE (forward) — a slow kill switch is flag-change propagation: streaming or polling and a stated reach bound, which this skill designs.
cases.reason: The stale value is a flag value, not a revoked grant of access; how flag changes reach every instance is the flag system's kill-switch propagation step.

cases.prompt: A customer downgraded from Enterprise yesterday but can still use audit export; find where the old plan is still held.
cases.note: SEAM CASE (reverse) — a plan downgrade that did not take effect is an access change still honored from a stale copy of authority.
cases.reason: authority-invalidation-architect owns making revoked roles, memberships and plan changes take effect everywhere authority is held; no flag is involved.
